skill.name: Same event, two tellers: how point of view changes a character
skill.why: The teller decides how a character looks to you. Different teller, different character.
skill.how: Read both tellings. Compare what each teller notices, leaves out, and says about the character.

beats.say: Two people can tell the same event very differently.

beats.show: Gus: I made a **brilliant diving save**. The crowd **went wild**.

beats.say: Now here's Tully telling the same thing.
beats.show: Tully: Gus **tripped over his shoelace**, and the ball **hit his bottom**.

beats.say: Same event! In Gus's telling he's a hero. In Tully's, he's clumsy.
Always ask: who's telling, and what do they want you to think?

creature.name: Duettle
creature.blurb: Twin turtle hatchlings from one nest who never tell a story the same way. Listen to both, and see who comes out the hero.

encounters.frame: Two Duettles heard a dog and a cat arguing on the beach.
encounters.text:
The dog's telling: The postie came to our gate. I barked and barked to keep my family safe. I am the bravest dog in the street. The postie ran away.

The cat's telling: The postie brought the letters, like always. The silly dog barked and barked. He knocked over his own water bowl. Then he hid under the couch. The postie laughed at him.
encounters.prompt: How does the dog seem in the cat's telling?
encounters.success: The cat calls him 'the silly dog'. In the dog's own telling, he's a hero.

options.reason: That's how the dog tells it. The cat says he hid under the couch.

options.reason: A dog that barks and barks isn't sleepy.

Mo's telling: Tully's kick went sideways. It hit a seagull, then the post. Then it bounced through for a goal. Tully bowed to the seagull. Coach laughed so hard he cried. The seagull was fine, just grumpy.

encounters.frame: Indi painted a mural. The principal has something to say about it.

Principal Hart's telling: On Monday morning, I found a huge purple octopus painted on the back wall. Nobody had asked permission. There was paint on the bins, the path and a very surprised possum. The artist had signed it, which made my job much easier. I have rung her parents.

encounters.text:
Captain Mortimer's ad: Dare you take the Twotide Ghost Walk? Your guide, the fearsome Captain Mortimer, has faced the Drowned Sailor three times and lived to tell the tale. Grown adults have fainted at his stories. Children have fled screaming into the night. Bring a torch, if you dare. Not for the faint-hearted! Tickets $15.

His 'terrifying' story about the Drowned Sailor was mostly about his own boat, which he is trying to sell. Halfway through the walk, a fruit bat flew past and he hid behind my nine-year-old son. My son had to hold his hand for the rest of the tour. The only scary thing all night was the price. The scones at the end were excellent.

encounters.frame: Leo cooked dinner. He and his nonna both told the Duettles about it.
encounters.text:
Leo's telling: Last night I cooked dinner for the whole family for the first time, all by myself. I made spaghetti with my own secret sauce. It took a while, but it was worth it. I wore Dad's apron and a proper chef's hat. Everyone said it was delicious, and Nonna even asked for the recipe. I think I might become a chef. Next week I'm making a pavlova.

Nonna's telling: Last night my grandson Leo cooked dinner. He used every pot in the kitchen and set off the smoke alarm twice. The 'secret sauce' was tomato sauce from a bottle, with a whole lot of pepper. We ate at ten o'clock, very hungry. The pepper made Grandad sneeze nine times. Leo smiled the whole time. I asked for the recipe so that nobody would ever make it again. Still, he did the washing-up without being asked, and I was proud of him.

encounters.frame: It's swooping season. The Duettles heard from a bike rider and a magpie.
encounters.text:
Sam's telling: I was riding my bike to school along the creek path, minding my own business, when I was attacked from above. A huge black-and-white monster dive-bombed my helmet seven times. Its beak clacked right next to my ear. I nearly fell off. I pedalled so fast that I won the race to school by a mile, and I wasn't even in a race. That bird is a menace and should be banned from the path. I've drawn a picture of it for the police.

The magpie's telling: My three chicks hatched last week in the nest above the creek path. This morning, a strange creature came racing towards them on a squeaking metal machine, wearing a shiny red shell on its head. I warned it seven times to stay away from my babies. It finally left at great speed. My chicks are safe. They have eaten four worms each. I am exhausted.

Zed's telling: The Twotide Kart Cup final was the hardest race of my life. On the last lap, Rex tried to block me on every corner, but I stayed calm and focused. My hands didn't shake once. The crowd groaned each time. After the race, Rex said, 'Good game, I guess.' Zed then did a victory dance on the library table and was asked to get down. He was also asked to stop calling himself a legend over the microphone. He refused.

encounters.frame: The school disco went dark. Two band members told the Duettles what happened.
encounters.text:
Ruby's telling: Our band, The Soggy Socks, played at the school disco on Friday. I'm the lead singer, so I had to hold everything together. The drummer kept losing his sticks, and the keyboard player forgot the chords. When the power went out halfway through our big song, I kept singing in the dark so the crowd wouldn't panic. Everyone said it was the best part of the night. I was a total professional.

Arlo's telling: Ruby sang so loudly at the disco that she blew the fuse on the speakers. She'd turned her microphone up to full volume when nobody was looking. When the power cut out, she kept singing anyway, in the pitch dark, for about ten minutes. She also did three costume changes by torchlight. Nobody panicked. Most people went to get a drink. Mr Fong had to find the fuse box with his phone torch. Mr Fong said it was certainly the loudest part of the night.

Commander Vale's log: Day 40. Today I performed a difficult spacewalk to repair the station's solar panel. Out in the freezing dark, I worked with steady hands and nerves of steel. The view of Earth was breathtaking, but I stayed focused on the job. When a tool floated away, I calmly carried on. The panel is working perfectly. Another job done. I am proud of my work.

She asked us four times whether anyone had seen it. She then held the panel together with tape for two hours, humming loudly into her microphone. She hummed the same song all the way through. The panel works. The spanner has been given a name by the team: Steve. Steve is doing well.

Maxx's voice-over: Deep in the sea caves of Twotide Atoll, a tiny Duettle hatchling was trapped and terrified, until I arrived. The tide was rising fast, and every second counted. Ignoring the danger, I squeezed between the jagged rocks and gently cradled the little guy in my hands. It was the most dangerous rescue of my career. I'll never forget its tiny face. The raw tape, written down by Zed: Waves crashing. Maxx is sitting on a dry rock, checking his teeth in a phone screen. A Goldie says, 'It's wedged behind that rock, boss.' For forty seconds, it squeaks sharply, the way frightened turtles do. Maxx covers his ears and says, 'Ugh. We'll put happy chirps over that in the studio.' Then he takes the net, holds it up to the drone and flashes his teeth. The hatchling is still squeaking. 'Are we rolling? Okay. Deep in the sea caves...'

encounters.frame: Tully wrote in her diary about the semi-final. Her coach wrote about it in the club newsletter.
encounters.text:
Tully's diary, Saturday: Worst. Coach. Ever. Coach Dunn benched me for the whole second half of the semi-final, for no reason at all, while the Reef Rays were losing. I sat on that freezing bench for forty minutes, watching Jess miss a goal I could have kicked with my eyes shut. She missed by a mile. The Reef Rays lost by four points, and the orange slices at half-time were the only good part. Then, after the siren, Coach made me pack up every single cone by myself. I am seriously thinking about switching clubs. Mum says I'm overreacting. Mum is wrong.

Reef Rays Under-12s newsletter, Coach Dunn's Corner: A tough loss in the semi-final, but I'm proud of every player. We lost by four points, but we never stopped trying. Special mention to Tully, who played a blinder in the first half before rolling her ankle in a tackle. We rested her for the second half to protect that ankle for next season, although she argued about it for most of the third quarter. Tully also kindly stayed back to help pack up the cones, even though she was limping. Thanks, Tully, and well done to Jess on her first semi-final. Training is on Tuesday at five. Bring a warm jumper.

encounters.frame: The Duettles found a newspaper story about a wombat. Then they heard from the wombat.
encounters.text:
From the Twotide Times: RAMPAGING WOMBAT TERRORISES CAMPERS. A family camping at Saltbush Point had a terrifying night on Saturday when a wild wombat attacked their tent. 'It came out of nowhere at two in the morning,' said camper Dev Kapoor. 'It dug straight through the floor, right under my sleeping bag, and then it just sat there glaring at me.' Mrs Kapoor said the children were too frightened to sleep for the rest of the night. Rangers say campers should always keep their distance from wombats. The Kapoors have gone home early. They had only arrived that afternoon.

The wombat's telling: I have lived in the same burrow at Saltbush Point for eleven years. On Saturday I went out for my evening grass, as I always do, and when I came home, somebody had put a giant flapping house right on top of my front door. I dug my way in, naturally. Inside, a large creature in a padded bag was lying across my doorway, snoring. I sat and waited politely for it to move. It screamed instead. Then the whole flapping house fell down around me, and everyone ran away. I have now had to dig a new back door, and I am very tired.

The milk had turned yellow, then green, then a colour I have no name for. When I opened the lid in the galley to collect a sample, a powerful gas was released, proving the experiment was a success. The smell was intense but scientifically important. Mo's reaction was emotional, which I have also recorded. I am the first person on this boat to achieve such a result. Next, I will try cheese. That's not gross. That's science.

Tully's message to the crew chat: Gus opened his three-week-old milk jar in the galley. With the hatches shut. The smell made Mo cry, and he was up on deck. Wren had to carry the fruit bowl outside with a peg on her nose. Zed climbed the mast and refused to come down. Gus refused to put the lid back on, because he said the gas was 'evidence'. Statistically, there is a 94 per cent chance the galley never smells normal again. I have hidden the jar. Do not ask me where.

DELIVERY BOT K-7, LOG: 14:02. Arrived at 12 Gull Street with one birthday cake. 14:03. Rang doorbell. No answer. 14:04. Checked address. Address correct. 14:05. Rang again. Detected large dog. Dog detected me. 14:06. Dog removed my front wheel. 14:07. Human opened door, shouting. Human did not say thank you. Human took cake and closed door. 14:09. Hopped home on one wheel. Journey took two hours. Customer rating: one star. Would not deliver again.

Mrs Brennan's letter to the delivery company: I am writing about the robot that delivered my daughter's birthday cake on Saturday. I was upstairs in the shower when it rang the bell, and I came down as fast as I could, wrapped in a towel. I had shampoo in my hair and one eye shut. By then, our dog, Biscuit, had already chewed off one of its wheels. I shouted at Biscuit to drop it, grabbed the cake and shut the door before he could do any more damage. I felt terrible. I am so embarrassed. Please tell the robot I'm sorry, and send me the bill for the wheel. The cake was perfect. My daughter says it was the best birthday ever, and Biscuit has been banned from the front yard.

encounters.frame: The school musical had a dramatic opening night. The Duettles read two tellings.
encounters.text:
Jasper's blog post: Opening night of Pirates of Twotide was a triumph, if I say so myself. As Captain Bluebeard, I had the biggest solo in the show, and I absolutely nailed it. My high note at the end was so powerful that the front row had to hold onto their seats. Halfway through, the ship's mast came crashing down behind me, but I didn't even flinch. I just kept singing, like a true professional. The audience gave me a standing ovation at the end. Honestly, I carried the whole show. Next stop: the big time.

The stage manager's report: Opening night went mostly to plan. During Bluebeard's solo, Jasper stepped back too far and knocked down the mast, which landed on the piano. Jasper kept singing, but he was facing the wrong way for the rest of the song, so the audience mostly saw the back of his hat. At the end, the audience stood up and cheered, mainly for the Year 3 parrots, who danced beautifully. Jasper's high note was mostly drowned out by the piano lid slamming shut. Next show: please stop Jasper bowing for three minutes after everyone else has left the stage. Also, someone please fix the mast.
